verses.note: Abram's wealth is real and is counted among God's blessings in later chapters (24:35), but this chapter shows at once that it brings pressure and conflict. Scripture treats possessions as gifts that must be held loosely, and the next verses show Abram doing exactly that.

Lot chose land by what his eyes saw (13:10), and the wealth he gathered there is the first thing he loses. The verse shows, without comment, how exposed a life becomes when its choices are made for gain.
Abram's tenth is the Bible's first tithe, given freely before any law required it. It is a confession that the spoils came from God; Jacob will make a similar vow in 28:22.
The servant presents Abraham's wealth not as achievement but as blessing: the LORD gave it. Scripture consistently treats riches as a gift held under God, as Deuteronomy 8:18 later reminds Israel.

Isaac's wealth is presented as a gift of the LORD, not an achievement, yet it immediately brings envy and conflict. The verse neither despises prosperity nor treats it as safe; blessing in the land still has to be lived out among resentful neighbors.

Jacob's tithe begins from the conviction that everything he will have is God's gift: ‘of all that You give me’. The tenth is a return of part of what is already received, which is how the rest of Scripture frames giving (1 Chronicles 29:14).
